summary.0: Chinese obstetrician admits to selling patients' newborns: Chinese obstetrician Zhang Shuxia admitted in court to stealing newborns from Fuping County Maternal and Child Hospital in Shaanxi Province and selling them to human traffickers. From November 2011 to July last year, she sold seven babies to middlemen who then sold them to couples in central and eastern China. One baby died after being trafficked for 1,000 yuan. Zhang was caught when a mother reported her suspicions to the police. The case has highlighted the issue of child trafficking in China and raised concerns about corruption in the medical profession. Several suspects have been detained in multiple provinces.
summary.1: Francis leads first Christmas celebrations as pope: Pope Francis led Christmas celebrations at Saint Peter's Basilica for the first time since his election as leader of the world's 1.2 billion Catholics. He conducted a solemn procession, personally placing a statue of baby Jesus in a manger. The Vatican also unveiled a Nativity scene and a Christmas tree from Bavaria. Francis urged Catholics to focus on the spiritual meaning of Christmas and emphasized the importance of silence amidst the festivities. On Wednesday, he will deliver traditional Christmas blessings and a multilingual message from the Vatican basilica's central balcony.
summary.2: Croatia arrests ex-spy chief wanted in Germany: Croatia arrested former intelligence chief Josip Perkovic, wanted in Germany for the 1983 murder of a Yugoslav dissident. Perkovic, along with 10 others, was arrested as Croatia aligned its extradition laws with the EU. Perkovic's lawyer stated he would oppose extradition, citing concerns over a fair trial in Germany. The amended law, removing a time limit on extradition, took effect on January 1. President Ivo Josipovic emphasized the law's equal application. Perkovic, a former UDBA member, awaits a local court ruling on extradition within eight days.
summary.3: ERNEST GAIL BAUER: Ernest Gail Bauer was born on October 7, 1921, in Clay County to Ernest and Pera (Nemnich) Bauer. He grew up in the Broughton community, graduated from CCCHS, and married Mina Oetinger on October 24, 1943. After farming in Broughton, they moved to Fairbury, Neb., in 1964, then returned to Clay Center in 1967. He worked for Gilmore-Tatge for 17 years before retiring and returning to farming. His first wife passed away on April 13, 1994, and he later married Dorothy (LeClair) Friesen on March 8, 1997. He was involved in various organizations and had several surviving family members. A funeral service will be held on December 21 at the Clay Center United Methodist Church, with burial in Broughton Cemetery. Visitation will be on December 20, with memorials suggested for the church or Clay Center Utility Park and Zoo.
summary.4: Justice delays health law's birth...: Justice Sonia Sotomayor blocked part of President Barack Obama's health care law requiring some religion-affiliated organizations to provide birth control in response to a request from the Little Sisters of the Poor Home for the Aged in Denver. The law's contraceptive coverage requirements were temporarily enjoined, giving the government until Friday to respond. The Catholic Church's opposition to contraceptives led to a conflict with the law's provisions. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit also issued an emergency stay for Catholic-affiliated groups challenging the contraceptive provision. The Supreme Court is set to rule on whether businesses can use religious objections to avoid covering birth control for employees, with a case involving Hobby Lobby Inc. scheduled for argument in March.
summary.5: Nate Silver - by: Erics Inner Monologue: Nate Silver stated that the United States has a statistical chance of advancing similar to Portugal. He predicts Italy has a 40% chance of qualifying and believes Chile will defeat Holland. Silver appears to favor CONCACAF and smaller South American teams, while discounting Croatia and Switzerland but favoring Bosnia and Russia. Randomly selecting results for middle-ranking teams could yield similar rankings.
summary.6: Croatian police arrest former top spy sought by Germany: Croatian police arrest former top spy Josip Perkovic sought by Germany for involvement in the 1983 murder of a Croatian dissident. Perkovic will oppose extradition to Germany, with a Zagreb court set to rule within eight days. Croatia amended its law on the European Arrest Warrant after a dispute with the EU, allowing for Perkovic's potential extradition. Speculation suggests reluctance to extradite Perkovic due to potential compromising information on Croatian politics and society. Government denies connection between law change and Perkovic's case, citing protection of veterans from EU investigations.
summary.7: DONALD WEHMHOFF: Donald Wehmhoff was born on June 19, 1921 in Clay County, the son of Louis and Katherine (Dagan) Wehmhoff. He married Lucille Stewart on Oct. 31, 1942 and served in the U.S. Army during World War II in Europe. After returning to Clay Center, he farmed and raised livestock for 26 years before becoming a real estate manager in Colorado, Utah, and Arizona in 1972. He returned to Clay Center in 1984 and worked as a crop insurance adjuster. He was a member of the First Presbyterian Church and served on the Co-op Board of Directors. Survivors include one daughter, Donice Rothfuss and husband Dennis of Winston-Salem, N.C.; two granddaughters; and three great-grandchildren. summary.844: Ionisation in atmospheres of brown dwarfs and extrasolar planets VI: Properties of large-scale discharge events. (arXiv:1312.6789v3 [astro-ph.EP] UPDATED): Abstract: Mineral clouds in substellar atmospheres act as catalysts for charge processes, leading to electrically activated environments with charged grains discharging through lightning events. These discharges impact local chemistry, potentially creating conditions conducive to early planetary life. By applying scaling laws to model atmospheres, we analyze the propagation and energetics of lightning and sprites through atmospheric clouds. Lightning discharges affect a larger atmospheric volume in a brown dwarf ($10^8 -~10^{10}$m$^3$) compared to a giant gas planet ($10^4 -~10^{6}$m$^3$). Our results indicate total dissipated energy in one event is <$10^{12}$ J for all solar metallicity models. Lightning influences gas phase composition, increasing small carbohydrate molecules while decreasing CO and CH$_4$. Dust forming molecules are destroyed, and cloud particle properties remain unchanged unless complete evaporation occurs. We also discuss potential instruments for observing lightning on extrasolar objects.
summary.845: The polluted atmospheres of cool white dwarfs and the magnetic field connection. (arXiv:1401.1249v1 [astro-ph.SR]): We present an analysis of X-Shooter spectra of the polluted hydrogen-rich white dwarfs NLTT 888 and NLTT 53908. The spectra of NLTT 53908 show strong, Zeeman-split calcium lines (CaII H&K and Ca I λ4226) and the star appears to be a close relative of the polluted magnetic white dwarf NLTT 10480, while the spectra of NLTT 888 show narrow lines of calcium and iron. A comparison of NLTT 888 and NLTT 53908 with other class members illustrates the diversity of environment and formation circumstances surrounding these objects. The incidence of magnetism in old, polluted white dwarfs significantly exceeds that found in the general white dwarf population, suggesting a hypothetical link between a crowded planetary system and magnetic field generation.

summary.1006: Central African Republic: Regional leaders to meet on future of C.Africa president: African leaders are set to meet in Chad on January 9, 2014, to discuss the future of Central African Republic President Michel Djotodia in an effort to address the sectarian violence in the country. The CAR has been in turmoil since rebels from the Seleka movement staged a coup in March, leading to Djotodia becoming the country's first Muslim president. Despite Djotodia's efforts to disband the rebels, violence has continued, resulting in over 1,000 deaths and nearly a million displaced individuals. Concerns have also been raised about the unrest spreading to neighboring countries, with reports of armed elements crossing into the Democratic Republic of Congo. While international military intervention has helped reduce mass killings, a sustainable political solution remains elusive. The possibility of Djotodia's departure is a contentious issue, with some warning that it could further destabilize the country. Additionally, challenges remain in organizing presidential elections and forming a national unity transitional government. summary.1811: Keystone pipeline clears hurdle: The controversial Keystone XL oil pipeline cleared a major hurdle on Friday as the State Department ruled the project wouldn't significantly increase greenhouse gas emissions. The Environmental Impact Statement on the project reiterates key parts of a draft analysis released early last year, finding that oil sands extraction would continue regardless of whether the pipeline is built. The finding could be crucial, as President Obama has said he would only approve the pipeline if he was convinced it would not "significantly exacerbate carbon emissions." The report also notes that a steep drop in oil prices, and "long-term constraints on any new pipeline capacity" -- and resulted in higher transportation costs of the oil -- then there could be a "substantial impact on oil sands production." On the other hand, the report states Keystone XL would transport 830,000 barrels of oil each day, adding an extra 1.3 million to 27.4 million metric tons of carbon dioxide to the atmosphere every year. While the report doesn't make the claim that Keystone would drastically "exacerbate emissions," it does state the crude oil will make it to market either way -- as a result Obama will have to determine if that oil will be burned even if he denies the project. The release marks the end of a five-year lobbying battle over the report on the environmental impact of Keystone, a project of TransCanada Corp. that would carry oil sands from Alberta to the Gulf Coast. The oil industry hailed State's findings, arguing they should lay to rest concerns about the pipeline. "Five years, five federal reviews, dozens of public meetings, over a million comments and one conclusion -- the Keystone XL pipeline is safe for the environment," said Jack Gerard, president and CEO of the American Petroleum Institute. "This final review puts to rest any credible concerns about the pipeline's potential negative impact on the environment. This long awaited project should now be swiftly approved. It's time to put thousands of Americans to work." Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio), a Keystone backer, said Obama is "out of excuses." "If President Obama wants to make this a 'year of action' he will stand up to the extreme Left in his own party, stand with the overwhelming majority of American people, and approve this critical project," Boehner said in a statement. But green groups, which are waging a national campaign to stop the pipeline, said the report bolsters their case by acknowledging that the pipeline could worsen climate change. summary.2351: Do You Need to Worry About the Netflix-Comcast Deal?: According to some estimates, Netflix accounts for more than 30% of all peak downstream Internet traffic in the U.S. With a user base of nearly 34 million U.S. subscribers and rapidly growing, Netflix has understandably generated some stress on the system, and streaming quality has been negatively affected lately. Under the new agreement, Netflix and Comcast will be eliminating the middlemen, in this case Cogent Communications, to establish "a more direct connection between Netflix and Comcast, similar to other networks, that's already delivering an even better user experience to consumers, while also allowing for future growth in Netflix traffic," according to the press release. Lowell McAdam, CEO of Verizon Communications, said in an interview with CNBC on Monday that Verizon and Netflix have been in conversations for more than a year over a similar agreement. According to Engadget, AT&T has confirmed it is also working on a more direct connection with Netflix, so the recently announced deal with Comcast is probably the first of many. This is not about net neutrality. Net neutrality is a hot issue lately, and many seem to be concerned about what this new announcement means in that respect. However, this deal is not about net neutrality. Net neutrality is about Internet service providers treating all Internet data equally, which means refraining from blocking, discriminating, or charging extra fees to different content, sites, or applications, for example. Net neutrality refers mostly to traffic traveling over a provider's last mile into consumer homes. Commercial interconnect relationships, or paid peering agreements, on the other hand, relate to the level at which different networks interconnect and how traffic is interchanged -- they are about content companies' networks and the edge of broadband access networks. In fact, big industry players like Google, Microsoft, and Facebook have traditionally engaged in this kind of agreement, and this has never raised much controversy on the net neutrality front. Someone needs to pay for growing connectivity needs, and it may as well be the companies making a lot of money online and accounting for a big chunk of traffic. Eliminating the intermediaries tends to generate economic efficiencies, so consumers could actually benefit from these agreements in the medium term. Economic terms of the agreement have not been disclosed, so it's hard to measure the direct financial impact for different companies involved. Comcast and other Internet service providers will likely be the major beneficiaries from a more direct relationship with Netflix, while intermediaries like Cogent look like the biggest losers from this kind of agreement. As for Netflix, some analysts are saying that costs could stay at similar levels, or even fall as the company will no longer have to pay Cogent Communications. It's worth noting that the deal was announced while Comcast is in the midst of its fusion with Time Warner, so perhaps the online streaming company had an advantage in the negotiations, as Comcast may not want to raise concerns from regulators regarding the company's market share and dominant competitive position. Besides, it's not all about costs for Netflix: Service quality is much more important as the company still has many years of growth ahead of it, so the priority should be making sure that customers get access to a high-quality streaming experience in order for Netflix to capitalize on its long-term opportunities for growth. From a financial point of view, variables like subscriber growth and content costs will probably have a much larger impact for Netflix than operating costs in the years ahead. The new deal between Netflix and Comcast is not related to net neutrality. If anything, consumers will likely benefit by receiving better service for a similar price. In addition, regardless of short-term cost considerations, Netflix is doing the right thing by focusing on customer experience. From the perspective of both consumers and investors in Netflix, this deal looks more like a positive development than a reason for concern.

summary.2621: Doctors hope for cure in a 2nd baby born with HIV: A second baby born with the AIDS virus may have had her infection put into remission and possibly cured by very early treatment - in this instance, four hours after birth. Doctors revealed the case Wednesday at an AIDS conference in Boston. The girl was born in suburban Los Angeles last April, a month after researchers announced the first case from Mississippi. That was a medical first that led doctors worldwide to rethink how fast and hard to treat infants born with HIV, and the California doctors followed that example. In another AIDS-related development, scientists have modified genes in the blood cells of a dozen adults to help them resist HIV. The results give hope that this approach might one day free at least some people from needing medicines to keep HIV under control, a form of cure. The Mississippi baby is now 3 1/2 and seems HIV-free despite no treatment for about two years. The Los Angeles baby is still getting AIDS medicines, so the status of her infection is not as clear. A host of sophisticated tests at multiple times suggest the Los Angeles baby has completely cleared the virus. The baby's signs are different from what doctors see in patients whose infections are merely suppressed by successful treatment. Doctors are cautious about suggesting she has been cured, but that's obviously their hope. Most HIV-infected moms in the U.S. get AIDS medicines during pregnancy, which greatly cuts the chances they will pass the virus to their babies. The Mississippi baby's mom received no prenatal care and her HIV was discovered during labor. Doctors started the baby on treatment 30 hours after birth, even before tests could determine whether she was infected. The Los Angeles baby was born at Miller Children's Hospital Long Beach, and "we knew this mother from a previous pregnancy" and that she was not taking her HIV medicines. The mom was given AIDS drugs during labor to try to prevent transmission of the virus, and the baby was started on them a few hours after birth. Tests later confirmed she had been infected, but does not appear to be now, nearly a year later. The baby is continuing treatment, is in foster care "and looking very healthy." The Mississippi girl was treated until she was 18 months old, when doctors lost contact with her. Ten months later when she returned, they could find no sign of infection even though the mom had stopped giving her AIDS medicines. Bryson is one of the leaders of a federally funded study just getting underway to see if very early treatment can cure HIV infection. About 60 babies in the U.S. and other countries will get very aggressive treatment that will be discontinued if tests over a long time, possibly two years, suggest no active infection. The study in adults was prompted by an AIDS patient who appears cured after getting a cell transplant seven years ago in Berlin from a donor with natural immunity to the virus. Only about 1 percent of people have two copies of the gene that gives this protection, and researchers have been seeking a more practical way to get similar results. HIV usually infects blood cells through a protein on their surface called CCR5. A California company, Sangamo BioSciences Inc., makes a treatment that can knock out a gene that makes CCR5. Dr. Carl June at the University of Pennsylvania tested it in 12 HIV patients who had their blood filtered to remove some of their cells. The treated cells were infused back into the patients. Four weeks later, half of the patients were temporarily taken off AIDS medicines to see the gene therapy's effect. The virus returned in all but one of them; that patient turned out to have one copy of the protective gene. The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases sponsored the work with Sangamo and Penn. Jay Johnson, 53, who works for Action AIDS, an advocacy and service organization in Philadelphia, had the treatment more than three years ago. Although the virus rebounded when he temporarily went off HIV medicines, tests show his modified blood cells are still multiplying. summary.2873: A needed Pac-12 Conference win for the Stanford men: Dwight Powell made one of two free throws with 36 seconds remaining to play to give the Stanford men's basketball team a 61-60 victory over visiting Utah in the Pac-12 Conference regular-season finale on Saturday. Chasson Randle scored 22 points to lead the Cardinal (10-8 Pac-12, 19-11 overall), which heads into the conference tournament next week in Las Vegas still waiting to find out its seed, which could wind up anywhere between No. 4 and No. 6 depending on the outcome of the Colorado-California game. A Colorado win means the Cardinal would receive the fourth seed. A California win means Stanford is seeded sixth and plays USC on Wednesday night in Las Vegas. The game played out as a microcosm of Stanford's season: looking good at one point, looking bad the next and just holding on despite itself at other times. Most observers feel the Cardinal nailed down a spot in the NCAA tournament, which would be the first time under Johnny Dawkins, but after needing a late turnover from then Utes to close out its win, Stanford may need a win in the conference tournament. The Cardinal has played on the brink of disaster all year, yet somehow finds a way to play itself back into contention. It happened again against Utah. The last 7:50 of the contest, save Powell's free throw, provided yet another example of how Stanford flirts with despair: NCAA style. Stefan Nastic, who made all six of his field goal attempts and finished with 14 points, gave Stanford a 54-43 lead with 7:51 left in the game. Utah responded with consecutive 3-pointers and a layup to close within 54-51 with 5:40 left. Stanford, meanwhile, forgot how to shoot. The Utes eventually took a 58-57 edge before Josh Huestis hit a 3-pointer with 2:19 left to put Stanford ahead to stay, just barely. The Cardinal was 1 of 4 from the field, 4 of 11 from the foul line and turned the ball over twice in the final 6:54. Since the September attack on an upscale mall that killed 67 people, Somali militant sympathizers have been blamed for an explosion at Nairobi's main airport, a grenade attack on tourists on Kenya's coast, a blast on a public bus in Nairobi, and three blasts Monday night in the capital that killed six people. A top police official who insisted on anonymity said security agencies believe a large attack is imminent. Police foiled a car bomb attack in Mombasa last month. Australia issued a weekend alert of "a serious and ongoing risk of large scale acts of terrorism" in Kenya. The U.S. Embassy last month reminded its citizens of the threat of terrorism.

summary.3291: City commuters stranded as matatus keep off roads | Nairobi News: City commuters in Nairobi were left stranded on Tuesday morning as matatus avoided the roads to evade arrest for non-compliance with new transport regulations. Some matatus operated briefly, charging double the usual fares before ceasing operations. Fares from Donholm to town rose to Sh100, while Roysambu fares reached Sh200. The new regulations, effective Tuesday morning, mandate the installation of digital speed governors in matatus. Matatu owners have criticized the high cost of the gadget, priced between Sh35,000 and Sh45,000. Despite the lack of police crackdown on non-compliant matatus, only 6,653 vehicles had been inspected nationwide as of the previous Saturday, far below the target of over 100,000. Approximately 21,000 digital speed governors had been imported by 16 approved suppliers. The Director of Motor Vehicle Inspection, Mr. Gerald Wangai, noted a recent surge in compliance after initial skepticism, with the workshop inspecting up to 200 vehicles daily and aiming for 500 on Monday. Long queues of vehicles were observed on Likoni, Enterprise, and Lunga Lunga roads as they awaited installation of the gadgets at the Industrial Area workshop.

summary.4678: Michelle Kaufman: CONCACAF finally being taken seriously by CONMEBOL: The opulent scene at the St. Regis Hotel in Bal Harbour on Thursday morning was the first sign that CONCACAF is finally flexing some muscle and being taken seriously by its neighboring Big Boy Confederation -- the South American CONMEBOL, home of heavyweights Brazil and Argentina.  Hundreds of sharply dressed dignitaries and soccer media stars showed up for the announcement of the long-rumored 2016 Copa America "Centenario," which will be hosted in the United States. The giant ballroom was decorated with fancy lighting, drapes and big video screens.   The highly coveted Copa America trophy was on display on the dais, as the presidents of the two confederations revealed their plans for the joint tournament.  Ten South American teams from CONMEBOL will be joined by six CONCACAF teams -- United States, Mexico and four others -- for a special off-year edition of the oldest continental tournament in the world.   The tournament will be held June 3-26, 2016, and is sure to fill stadiums across the United States.  Sun Life Stadium, with its history of near-sellouts for international matches, is likely to be chosen as a venue. The timing isn't ideal, as it will overlap with the European Championship, which has a sizable TV viewership in the Americas.   It also comes just one year after the regularly scheduled 2015 Copa America and 2015 Gold Cup.   World Cup qualifying matches also could fall during that June. And, maybe most troubling of all, FIFA has yet to put the Copa America "Centenario" on its official calendar.   Unless that happens, clubs will not be obligated to release their players.  Then, of course, there's the issue of the Major League Soccer season, which unlike the rest of the world, runs through the summer. But organizers seem confident all that will be worked out, and there is no question the event will get huge crowds and TV viewership.   Copa America already is a prestigious event and very popular with fans in the rest of the Americas, and the addition of the U.S. team, Mexico and four other teams from the Caribbean, Central and North America will make it even more appealing.  CONCACAF president Jeffrey Webb was correct when he declared that this would truly be a "Copa America" rather than just a Copa of South America. And CONMEBOL president Eugenio Figueredo talked glowingly of a "more permanent alliance" between the confederations in the future.  What, exactly, did he mean by that?  Will they go a step further and merge the two confederations?   Will they consider adding South America's 10 member nations to the 41 CONCACAF nations and making a 51-member mega-Pan American confederation, similar to Europe's 54-member UEFA?  While they're at it, why not scrap the Gold Cup?   Although it has gained some prestige in recent years, it lacks the drama and depth of Copa America.   Yes, it gives regional minnows such as Belize and Martinique a chance to compete and make some money, but they could still do that if Copa America expands its field and hosts qualifying rounds.  It's no different from Andorra, Moldova and the Faroe Islands playing in UEFA. And, how about adding club teams from CONCACAF nations into the Copa Libertadores instead of relegating MLS and Mexican club teams to the CONCACAF Champions League, which, let's face it, few fans seem to care about.  I could see a day when the Copa America is just like the European Championship, with regional group stages to weed out the weaker teams and then maybe a 16-team knockout stage.   The teams from the United States, Mexico, Honduras and Costa Rica surely would benefit from regular competition against the likes of Brazil, Argentina, Colombia and Uruguay.  Travel would be tough because the distance between Canada and Argentina, for example, is three times the distance between any two European countries.   But, based on the buzz in that hotel ballroom Thursday, it would be worth it.  * Miami World Cup tuneups: South Florida fans don't have to travel to Brazil this summer to see World Cup teams.   Five World Cup teams will play warmup matches at Sun Life Stadium on their way to Brazil.  England plays Ecuador on June 4 and then takes on Honduras on June 7.   The Honduran team will set up a training camp in Sunrise in mid-May and train there until the World Cup.  Ghana, which is in the same group as the United States in the World Cup, comes through Miami and plays South Korea at Sun Life Stadium on June 9.  Tickets are on sale through Ticketmaster and the stadium box office.  Further up the state, Japan plays Costa Rica on June 2 in Tampa, and the U.S. team plays Nigeria on June 7 in Jacksonville.  * Miami United Opener: Miami United FC, a third-tier pro team, opens its season Sunday against the Tampa Mauraders at 7 p.m. at Milander Park in Hialeah.   The team is coached by Ferdinando de Matthaus, who played alongside Pelé with the New York Cosmos, and former Miami Fusion star Diego Serna.   The team plays in the National Professional Soccer League.

Charles Warner's execution, originally scheduled for the same evening as Lockett's, has been postponed until November 13. Warner was sentenced to death for the rape and murder of his girlfriend's 11-month-old baby.
summary.4823: SDLP promise a change for the better: SDLP candidate Conor Quinn asserts that the party will bring significant positive change in the upcoming elections. summary.4824: NBA: Clippers' Crawford wins Sixth Man Award: NBA: Los Angeles Clippers guard Jamal Crawford wins Sixth Man Award for the 2013-2014 season. Crawford, a two-time winner, led all NBA reserves in scoring with 18.6 points per game. He received 57 first-place votes and a total of 421 points from a panel of 125 sportswriters and broadcasters. Crawford came off the bench in 45 of 69 games played, contributing to the Clippers' 57-25 record and No. 3 seed in the Western Conference playoffs.
summary.4825: Calif. Governor Brown Announces Appointments for May 7, 2014 including to California Department of Child Support Services: On May 7, 2014, Calif. Governor Edmund G. Dan Burch, a Republican from Turlock, was reappointed to the California Commission on Emergency Medical Services. John Buck, a Democrat from Folsom, was reappointed to the California Mental Health Services Oversight and Accountability Commission. Jacqueline Jackson, a Democrat from San Diego, was appointed to the California State Rehabilitation Council. Rosanna Johansen, a Democrat from Redding, was reappointed to Area Board II of the California State Council on Developmental Disabilities.
summary.4826: Oklahoma delays execution after botched lethal injection: Oklahoma's attorney general has agreed to delay Charles Warner's execution for six months following the botched lethal injection of Clayton Lockett. The state plans to reschedule Warner's execution for Nov. 13 pending a review of execution protocols by the public safety commissioner. The governor has committed to staying all executions until the review is completed. Warner's attorneys had requested a six-month stay after Lockett's execution went wrong, and they hope for an indefinite stay pending the state review. Oklahoma has faced criticism for its new lethal injection drug mix, with witnesses describing Lockett's execution as disturbing. President Obama has ordered a review of how states carry out the death penalty. Warner's attorneys have been trying to obtain information on the lethal injection drugs but have faced challenges due to the state's refusal to disclose the source.
summary.4827: Clippers' Jamal Crawford wins 2013-14 Kia NBA Sixth Man Award: Clippers' Jamal Crawford wins 2013-14 Kia NBA Sixth Man Award. Crawford led all NBA reserves in scoring, averaging 18.6 points. He also accounted for 3.2 apg and 2.3 rpg in 30.3 mpg. Crawford received 57 first-place votes and 421 total points. Taj Gibson finished second with 395 points and Manu Ginobili finished third with 138 points. Crawford tallied double-figure scoring efforts in 15-of-16 January games and posted 20-plus points 29 times and 30-plus points six times. summary.4828: Clippers' Jamal Crawford wins NBA's sixth-man award: Clippers' Jamal Crawford becomes oldest player to win NBA's sixth-man award, first to win with two teams. Crawford led all reserve players with 18.6 points per game, setting a team record with 161 three-pointers. Received 57 first-place votes and 421 total points.
summary.4829: Tennis: Murray bows out in Madrid: Murray lost to Giraldo in Madrid, unable to match his opponent's power and accuracy. Nadal defeated Nieminen but struggled with consistency. Nishikori advanced to the quarter-finals after beating Raonic.

summary.4831: Bill Requiring Smart Phone Kill Switches Clears California Senate: Bill Requiring Smart Phone Kill Switches Clears California Senate. Democratic State Senator Mark Leno advocates for pre-installed and active kill switches in smart phones to deter theft. Leno highlights the increasing number of smart phone thefts, with 1.6 million stolen in 2012 and doubled by 2013. San Francisco reports two-thirds of all robberies involve smart phones. The Wireless Association supports a nation-wide technological approach for customers to activate kill switches. Apple and Microsoft dropped opposition to the bill after tablets were excluded. The law's roll-out date is postponed from next January to next July.
summary.4832: State Senate passes cell phone kill switch legislation: California State Senate passed a bill requiring all smartphones sold in the state to have kill switches activated, aimed at reducing street robberies. The bill, authored by San Francisco Democratic Sen. Mark Leno, received 26-8 votes and was sent to the Assembly. Law enforcement agencies and organizations supported the bill, citing the need to combat smartphone thefts. The wireless industry, including major manufacturers Apple and Microsoft, initially opposed the bill but later withdrew their opposition. The bill's proponents argue that the kill switch feature would deter thefts by rendering stolen phones inoperable. The industry association CTIA proposed optional kill switches as an alternative, criticizing state mandates as stifling innovation.
summary.4833: National Basketball Association roundup: Shelly Sterling has hired a law firm to help her as the National Basketball Association (NBA) moves to terminate her husband's ownership of the team for making racist comments, as reported by the Los Angeles Times on Wednesday. Andersen stated, "You're going to need a body bag to keep me from playing."
summary.4834: Crawford wins 6th man award: Jamal Crawford of the Los Angeles Clippers wins the NBA's Sixth Man of the Year award for the 2013-14 season, marking his second win after previously receiving the honor in 2009-10 with Atlanta. Crawford led all reserves in scoring with an average of 18.6 points in 69 games, helping the Clippers secure the third seed in the Western Conference playoffs with a 57-25 record. He received 57 first-place votes and 421 points to beat out Taj Gibson of Chicago for the award.
summary.4835: Schulz vows to tackle gender pay gap: Martin Schulz vows to tackle the gender pay gap in the EU if elected as the next President of the European Commission. He emphasized the need to address the significant pay disparity between men and women, proposing to have an equal number of female and male commissioners in his team. Schulz also outlined plans to boost economic growth, including setting up an investment bank for SMEs in southern Europe and cracking down on tax avoidance. Despite facing competition from Jean-Claude Juncker, Schulz remains committed to combating euroscepticism and ensuring a fair democratic process in the EU elections.
summary.4836: Tennis: Murray bows out in Madrid, rusty Nadal through: Tennis: Andy Murray lost to Santiago Giraldo in Madrid, while Rafa Nadal advanced despite showing signs of rustiness. summary.4837: Odds on Federer twins at Wimbledon: News that Roger Federer and his wife, Mirka, welcomed twin boys on Tuesday, joining the 4-year-old twin girls they already have, led Ladbrokes to offer odds of 10,000 to 1 for the four Federer siblings to meet in a mixed doubles Wimbledon final. Abstract: The California Senate passed a revised version of the kill-switch bill requiring anti-theft technology in all new smartphones after tech giants Apple and Microsoft dropped their opposition. The bill mandates kill-switch technology in cellphones manufactured after July 1, 2015, and sold in California. The bill aims to combat the rise in violent smartphone robberies, with other states considering similar legislation. Law enforcement officials support the bill, emphasizing its potential to reduce armed robberies. Despite opposition from wireless carriers, the bill passed the Senate with amendments giving manufacturers six months to comply. The bill's sponsor, Sen. Mark Leno, highlighted the importance of addressing concerns to achieve success. The bill faces further review in the state Assembly, with ongoing discussions to address potential shortcomings, such as the impact on domestic violence victims.
summary.4842: California Senate Passes Bill Requiring Smartphone Kill Switches: California Senate passed a bill requiring smartphones sold in the state to have remote kill switches for theft prevention. The new bill, set to take effect in July 2015, was modified to allow more time for implementation and exclude tablets. Apple dropped its opposition, leading to the bill's passage. The state's influence on industry regulations is significant, with companies often complying with California's stricter rules. Smartphone theft is a major issue, especially in cities like New York and San Francisco, where iPhones are popular targets. Law enforcement has long advocated for kill switch technology to deter theft. Despite a voluntary agreement by smartphone makers to include kill switches by 2015, the bill sponsor deemed it insufficient. Apple already offers a remote kill switch through iCloud, but the bill will make it mandatory.
summary.4843: “Kill Switch” survives California Senate after all: "Kill Switch" legislation in California has passed the State Senate with an overwhelmingly positive vote of 26 to 8. San Francisco District Attorney George Gascon and State Senator Mark Leno sponsored the bill in response to rampant theft issues. Industry group CTIA and some California lawmakers have expressed concerns about the bill's necessity and potential impact on tech companies.

BBL braces for lower net profit in 2014: Title: BBL braces for lower net profit in 2014
Abstract: Bangkok Bank, Thailand's largest lender, anticipates a decrease in profits for 2014 due to reduced borrowing by business clients. The bank's first-quarter net profit declined by 0.5% compared to the previous year, with Moody's Investors Service projecting a slump in profits for Thai banks amidst political unrest. BBL's president expects the net profit to be lower than last year's Bt35.91 billion, primarily relying on corporate customers for profitability. Despite a slowdown in demand, the bank aims for loan growth of 3-5%, with a focus on clients in manufacturing and export sectors. Bangkok Life Assurance, a BBL subsidiary, also faces challenges in premium income growth due to political unrest, projecting a total premium growth of 25% for the year. summary.4860: Consumer confidence sinks, lowest since Nov 2001: UTCC: Consumer confidence in Thailand hit its lowest point since November 2001, with the Consumer Confidence Index (CCI) dropping to 67.8 in April, according to the University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce (UTCC). The negative economic growth of minus-1 per cent in the first quarter, coupled with ongoing political uncertainty, has raised concerns about a possible economic recession. Factors such as slower export recovery, a decline in tourism, and low crop prices have contributed to the economic downturn. The absence of a permanent government, delayed payments to farmers, and political tension have further dampened consumer confidence and economic growth prospects. If the political situation persists, economic growth is expected to remain below 2 per cent this year and only reach 0-3 per cent in 2015. However, the establishment of a permanent government by the third quarter could lead to GDP growth of 2-3 per cent this year and around 4 per cent in 2015.

summary.4955: CHARLES KRAUTHAMMER: Benghazi: How to do the hearings right: The Democrats are portraying the not-yet-even-constituted House Select Committee on Benghazi as nothing but a partisan exercise. They are even considering boycotting the hearings to delegitimize them. Fine. Although this would give the Obama-protective media a further reason to ignore Benghazi, it doesn't matter. All that matters is whether the committee produces new, important facts. If it does, it will be impossible to ignore. We've already seen what a single piece of new evidence can do in reviving interest in a story that many (including me) thought the administration had successfully stonewalled. The "PREP CALL with Susan [Rice]" email from Ben Rhodes, the deputy national security adviser, was withheld eight months until revealed by court order. It advises the U.N. ambassador to focus on an anti-Islam Internet video, thus contradicting the perennial White House claim that Rice's blame-the-video five-show fable came just from intelligence community talking points and not from a White House in full campaign mode. The select committee will be headed by Rep. Trey Gowdy, R-S.C C., a skilled 16-year prosecutor. He needs to keep the hearings clean and strictly fact-oriented. Questions only, no speechifying. Every sentence by every GOP committee member must end with a question mark. Should any committee Republican instead make a statement ending in a period, the chairman should immediately, by button, deliver an electric shock through the violator's seat. The areas of inquiry are obvious. They are three: before, during and after. Where and to what extent was there dereliction of duty as memos, urgent pleas and mounting evidence of danger were ignored and the U.S. ambassador allowed to enter a deathtrap? What happened during the eight hours of the Benghazi attack, at the end of which the last two Americans (of four) were killed by mortar fire? Where was the commander in chief and where was the responsible Cabinet secretary, Hillary Clinton? What did they do? The White House acts as if these are, alternatively, either state secrets or of no importance. For President Barack Obama, we have three data points. At 5 p.m. EDT, he is briefed about the attack by the secretary of defense and chairman of the Joint Chiefs. Around 8 p.m., Obama spends an hour on the phone with Benjamin Netanyahu to tamp down a breaking, politically injurious story that Obama had snubbed the Israeli prime minister. The White House then issues a readout saying the two leaders had agreed there had been no snub. So the White House is engaged in campaign damage control quite literally in the middle of the Benghazi events -- at a time when Ambassador Chris Stevens is still missing and the final firefight that killed two other Americans is still three hours away. We've just learned that Obama was not in the Situation Room that night. Then where, doing what? We know, finally, that at 10 p.m. Obama called Clinton to get an update. What did they discuss, decide, order? As former prosecutor Andrew McCarthy has pointed out, a half-hour later, State issued a statement deploring the video, setting the premise for the video excuse. Were Obama and Clinton working on a cover story -- even before Glen Doherty had joined Tyrone Woods on the roof of the CIA annex where they were to die minutes later? Yes, that's speculation. Well, then, give us facts. After all, the White House provided a cascade of hagiographic facts about Obama's involvement in the Osama bin Laden raid. Yet regarding Benghazi -- the most serious operational challenge of his presidency -- he is nowhere to be seen. We now know the White House was pushing the "video made them do it" cover-up, lest the blame be placed on administration policy. Who was involved in that decision, obviously designed to protect a president campaigning that al-Qaida was "on the run"? These hearings are a big political risk for Republicans. Going into the 2014 election, they stand to benefit from the major issues -- Obamacare, the economy, chronic unemployment -- from which Benghazi hearings can only distract. Worse, if botched like previous hearings on the matter, these hearings could backfire against the GOP, as did the 1998 Clinton impeachment proceedings. On purely partisan considerations, the hearings are not worth the political risk. But the country deserves the truth. They'll get it if the GOP can keep the proceedings clean, factual and dispassionate. No speeches. No grandstanding. Gowdy has got to be a tough disciplinarian -- especially toward his own side of the aisle.

summary.5007: CHARLES KRAUTHAMMER: Getting answers on Benghazi is important: The Democrats are portraying the not-yet-even constituted House Select Committee on Benghazi as nothing but a partisan exercise. They are even considering boycotting the hearings to delegitimize them. Fine. Although this would give the Obama-protective media a further reason to ignore Benghazi, it doesn't matter. All that matters is whether the committee produces new, important facts. If it does, it will be impossible to ignore. We've already seen what a single piece of new evidence can do in reviving interest in a story that many (including me) thought the administration had successfully stonewalled. The "PREP CALL with Susan [Rice]" email from Ben Rhodes, the deputy national security adviser, was withheld eight months until revealed by court order. It advises the U.N. ambassador to focus on an anti-Islam Internet video, thus contradicting the perennial White House claim that Rice's blame-the-video five-show fable came just from intelligence community talking points and not from a White House in full campaign mode. The select committee will be headed by Rep. Trey Gowdy, a skilled 16-year prosecutor. He needs to keep the hearings clean and strictly fact-oriented. Questions only, no speechifying. Every sentence by every GOP committee member must end with a question mark. Should any committee Republican instead make a statement ending in a period, the chairman should immediately, by button, deliver an electric shock through the violator's seat. The areas of inquiry are obvious. They are three: before, during and after. Where and to what extent was there dereliction of duty as memos, urgent pleas and mounting evidence of danger were ignored and the U.S. ambassador allowed to enter a deathtrap? What happened during the eight hours of the Benghazi attack, at the end of which the last two Americans (of four) were killed by mortar fire? Where was the commander in chief and where was the responsible Cabinet secretary, Hillary Clinton? What did they do? The White House acts as if these are, alternatively, either state secrets or of no importance. For President Obama, we have three data points. At 5 p.m. EDT, he is briefed on the attack by the secretary of defense and chairman of the Joint Chiefs. At around 8 p.m., Obama spends an hour on the phone with Benjamin Netanyahu to tamp down a breaking, politically injurious story that Obama had snubbed the Israeli prime minister. The White House then issues a readout saying the two leaders had agreed there had been no snub. So the White House is engaged in campaign damage control quite literally in the middle of the Benghazi events -- at a time when Ambassador Chris Stevens is still missing and the final firefight that killed two other Americans is still three hours away. We've just learned that Obama was not in the Situation Room that night. Then where, doing what? We know, finally, that at 10 p.m. Obama called Clinton to get an update. What did they discuss, decide, order? As former prosecutor Andrew McCarthy has pointed out, a half-hour later, State issued a statement deploring the video, setting the premise for the video excuse. Were Obama and Clinton working on a cover story -- even before Glen Doherty had joined Tyrone Woods on the roof of the CIA annex where they were to die minutes later? Yes, that's speculation. Well, then, give us facts. After all, the White House provided a cascade of hagiographic facts about Obama's involvement in the Osama bin Laden raid. Yet regarding Benghazi -- the most serious operational challenge of his presidency -- he is nowhere to be seen. We now know the White House was pushing the "video made them do it" cover-up, lest the blame be placed on administration policy. Who was involved in that decision, obviously designed to protect a president campaigning that al-Qaeda was "on the run"? These hearings are a big political risk for Republicans. Going into the 2014 election, they stand to benefit from the major issues -- Obamacare, the economy, chronic unemployment -- from which Benghazi hearings can only distract. Worse, if botched like previous hearings on the matter, these hearings could backfire against the GOP, as did the 1998 Clinton impeachment proceedings. On purely partisan considerations, the hearings are not worth the political risk. But the country deserves the truth. They'll get it if the GOP can keep the proceedings clean, factual and dispassionate. No speeches. No grandstanding. Gowdy has got to be a tough disciplinarian -- especially toward his own side of the aisle. Charles Krauthammer is a Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist email address is letters@charleskrauthammer.com.

summary.5078: Krauthammer: How to do the Benghazi hearings right: The Democrats are portraying the not-yet-even constituted House Select Committee on Benghazi as nothing but a partisan exercise. They are even considering boycotting the hearings to delegitimize them. Fine. Although this would give the Obama-protective media a further reason to ignore Benghazi, it doesn't matter. All that matters is whether the committee produces new, important facts. If it does, it will be impossible to ignore. We've already seen what a single piece of new evidence can do in reviving interest in a story that many (including me) thought the administration had successfully stonewalled. The "PREP CALL with Susan Rice" email from Ben Rhodes, the deputy national security adviser, was withheld eight months until revealed by court order. It advises the U.N. ambassador to focus on an anti-Islam Internet video, thus contradicting the perennial White House claim that Rice's blame-the-video five-show fable came just from intelligence community talking points and not from a White House in full campaign mode. The select committee will be headed by Rep. Trey Gowdy, a skilled 16-year prosecutor. He needs to keep the hearings clean and strictly fact-oriented. Questions only, no speechifying. The areas of inquiry are obvious. They are three: before, during and after. Before: Where and to what extent was there dereliction of duty as memos, urgent pleas and mounting evidence of danger were ignored and the U.S. ambassador allowed to enter a deathtrap? During: What happened during the eight hours of the Benghazi attack, at the end of which the last two Americans (of four) were killed by mortar fire? Where was the commander in chief, and where was the responsible Cabinet secretary, Hillary Clinton? What did they do? The White House acts as if these are, alternatively, either state secrets or of no importance. For President Obama, we have three data points. At 5 p.m. EDT, he is briefed on the attack by the secretary of defense and chairman of the Joint Chiefs. At around 8 p.m., Obama spends an hour on the phone with Benjamin Netanyahu to tamp down a breaking, politically injurious story that Obama had snubbed the Israeli prime minister. So the White House is engaged in campaign damage control quite literally in the middle of the Benghazi events -- at a time when Ambassador Chris Stevens is still missing and the final firefight that killed two other Americans is still three hours away. We know, finally, that at 10 p.m. Obama called Clinton to get an update. What did they discuss, decide, order? As former prosecutor Andrew McCarthy has pointed out, a half-hour later, State issued a statement deploring the video, setting the premise for the video excuse. Were Obama and Clinton working on a cover story -- even before Glen Doherty had joined Tyrone Woods on the roof of the CIA annex where they were to die minutes later? We now know the White House was pushing the "video made them do it" cover-up, lest the blame be placed on administration policy. Who was involved in that decision, obviously designed to protect a president campaigning that al-Qaeda was "on the run"? These hearings are a big political risk for Republicans. Going into the 2014 election, they stand to benefit from the major issues -- Obamacare, the economy, chronic unemployment -- from which Benghazi hearings can only distract. Worse, if botched like previous hearings on the matter, these hearings could backfire against the GOP, as did the 1998 Clinton impeachment proceedings. On purely partisan considerations, the hearings are not worth the political risk. But the country deserves the truth.

Monsegur's cooperation helped authorities infiltrate LulzSec, leading to successful prosecutions. Anonymous criticized Monsegur and the FBI, accusing them of criminal activities and creating examples to suppress dissent.
summary.5731: EU election: France's Hollande calls for reform of 'remote' EU: EU election: France's Hollande calls for reform of 'remote' EU. French President Francois Hollande emphasizes the need for the EU to scale back its power and simplify its structure in response to the rise of Eurosceptic and far-right parties. Hollande stresses the importance of focusing on boosting the economy and prioritizing growth, jobs, and investment within the EU. Meanwhile, France's far-right National Front secures victory in the European Parliament election, pushing Hollande's Socialists into third place. In a separate development, France's main opposition leader Jean-Francois Cope agrees to resign amidst pressure over financial irregularities and the UMP party's poor performance in the election. This paves the way for a new candidate selection process for the 2017 presidential election.
summary.5732: Beyonce trailer triggers film plea: Fans have launched a petition on Change.org to support a feature-length version of Run, a trailer starring Beyonce and Jay Z as gun-toting outlaws. The trailer includes cameos by Sean Penn, Don Cheadle, and Blake Lively, ending with the words "coming never". Beyonce and Jay Z are set to begin their On the Run concert tour next month in Miami, Florida. Last week, TMZ posted footage of a physical brawl between Jay Z and Beyonce's sister, Solange Knowles, which the trio stated they had "worked through".
summary.5733: Charlotte listens to regulation ideas for ride-share cars: The City of Charlotte's safety committee is considering regulations for ride-sharing services like Uber and Lyft to co-exist with taxi and limo companies. Uber Charlotte General Manager, David Salsone, highlighted the company's growth and transparency in surge pricing. Local limousine service owner, Tom Holden, argues that current rules create an uneven playing field. Concerns include verifying compliance standards and potential insurance gaps. The committee aims to make a recommendation by the summer.
summary.5734: Jury finds cleric al-Masri guilty in terror trial: A federal jury in New York found radical Islamic cleric Abu Hamza al-Masri guilty of aiding terrorists in incidents worldwide, facing 11 criminal counts. The jury deliberated for over 12 hours, convicting al-Masri on all counts. Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara described him as a "trainer of terrorists." Al-Masri testified his maiming was from an engineering accident, not battle. Defense criticized the prosecution's approach. Al-Masri denied involvement in a failed jihad training camp in Oregon, claiming to be a "mouthpiece." Prosecution presented videos of him endorsing violence. Al-Masri was convicted in the UK for inciting racial hatred.
summary.5735: Eurosceptic parties cause "earthquake" at EU polls: "Eurosceptic parties, including France's National Front and Britain's UKIP, caused a significant impact in the EU parliamentary polls, winning around 140 seats in the 751-seat assembly. The far-right National Front secured 24 seats in France, while UKIP achieved a historic victory in the UK. Projections show the European People's Party maintaining its top spot with 212 seats, followed by the Socialists with 187 seats. Despite concerns about anti-EU parties holding Parliament hostage, analysts suggest such fears may be exaggerated. European Commission head Jose Manuel Barroso called for pro-EU groups to unite, emphasizing the need to address the perceived 'democratic deficit' within the EU."
summary.5736: Don't bury European nationalism just yet: The European nationalist sentiment has resurfaced in the recent European Parliament elections, with voters expressing a lack of trust in pro-Europe parties. Economic dissatisfaction, high unemployment rates, and concerns about immigration have fueled this resurgence. Despite this, EU leaders continue to push for further integration, ignoring public skepticism. The article highlights the failure of the EU to eliminate nationalism and the growing discontent among European citizens.
summary.5737: The Fight to Win the Confidence of the Continent Reuters/Luke MacGregor: Elections to the European parliament ended with right-wing parties making significant gains across the Continent, challenging the political mainstream. The rise of populist politics and dissatisfaction with the EU's recovery strategy highlight the need for urgent attention to address voter alienation. The clash between neoliberal economic thinking and social-democratic beliefs presents a critical confrontation that must be addressed. The EU must respond to the seismic shift in voter sentiment and work towards regaining the confidence of the Continent.
summary.5738: Post-election blues grip European leaders: Post-election blues grip European leaders as anti-EU parties rise in UK, France, Denmark, Greece, and Italy. Despite Eurosceptics doubling their representation in the European Parliament, pro-European groups maintain control. Mainstream parties consider anti-immigration legislation to regain lost votes. Former UK PM Tony Blair urges louder pro-Europe stance and warns against reactionary forces. Mr. Blair emphasizes the importance of cooperation among nation states within Europe. UK PM Cameron urges European leaders to acknowledge the need for EU reform post-election results.
summary.5739: Leaders stunned as voters reject united Europe: Leaders in Europe were shocked by the rejection of a united Europe by voters in the recent European Parliament elections. The rise of once-fringe parties opposed to European integration has presented a reality check to mainstream parties. Economic struggles, particularly in countries like Greece, have fueled backlash against tough fiscal austerity measures. The outcome of the elections signals a potential shift towards reclaiming national powers from Brussels, with anti-EU parties making significant gains. Despite this, pro-EU parties may collaborate more closely to advance integration efforts. The surge of fringe groups could impact key legislation, such as the Free Trade Agreement with the United States.
summary.5740: Slush fund scandal hits Sarkozy hopes: France's main opposition party, the Union for a Popular Movement (UMP), is facing a financial scandal that has led to the resignation of its leader, Jean François Copé. The scandal involves allegations of illegal financing of Nicolas Sarkozy's 2012 presidential campaign. Marine Le Pen, leader of the National Front, sees this as an opportunity to further her political ambitions.
summary.5741: FBI informer Hector Xavier Monsegur helps halt over 300 cyber attacks: FBI informer Hector Xavier Monsegur, also known as Sabu, has played a crucial role in preventing over 300 cyber attacks since his arrest. He admitted involvement in major hacking attacks in 2011 against Sony Pictures Entertainment, Fox Broadcasting Company, and PBS. Monsegur, a member of the Anonymous hacktivist collective LulzSec, has assisted in key arrests, prosecutions, and convictions in the US, UK, and elsewhere. Prosecutors have recommended leniency for Monsegur, who faces a potential prison sentence of up to 26 years but has already served seven months in jail.
summary.5742: China and Russia sign gas deal (Updated): China and Russia signed a $400-billion gas supply deal on Wednesday, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping witnessing the agreement between Gazprom and China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) in Shanghai. The deal, marking the largest in the history of the former USSR, will see Russia deliver gas to China via a new pipeline starting in 2018, gradually reaching 38 billion cubic meters annually. The contract, which includes $20 billion from China for gas development and infrastructure, aims to reduce China's reliance on coal and aid in its "war on pollution." The agreement also presents an opportunity for Gazprom to enter the Asian LNG market, with plans to build a new LNG plant near Vladivostok.
summary.5743: French opposition leader quits amid scandal: The scandal-ridden French opposition party, the UMP, faced a crisis as party leader Jean-François Copé resigned amid revelations of a funding scandal for Nicolas Sarkozy's failed 2012 election campaign. The UMP leadership agreed to step down on June 15th after reports of illegal billing of campaign expenses. The scandal involved routing money through a communication agency run by Copé's allies, leading to accusations of falsifying invoices. Sarkozy's ex-deputy campaign director admitted to exceeding spending limits but denied embezzlement. The UMP's existence was threatened last year due to spending limit violations. Sarkozy appealed for donations to save the party, emphasizing the need for a political alternative to socialism. Sarkozy, implicated in corruption scandals, expressed unhappiness over being dragged into the affair. The funding scandal added to the UMP's woes following a defeat by the National Front party in the European elections.
summary.5744: LulzSec 'Leader' Sabu Helped Feds Stop 300 Attacks: US law enforcement agencies prevented at least 300 cyber attacks with help from Hector Monsegur, also known as Sabu, the apparent leader of LulzSec. Monsegur provided information on vulnerabilities that could have been exploited against the US government, including NASA and Congress, as well as a water utility in a US city and a foreign energy company. His assistance led to the identification, prosecution, and conviction of eight major co-conspirators, including the arrest of Jeremy Hammond. Monsegur's actions resulted in the prevention of millions of dollars in losses. The US government has requested a reduced sentence for Monsegur due to his substantial cooperation.
summary.5745: Europe's Leaders Meet to Analyse Eurosceptic Poll Wins: "European leaders convene in Brussels to analyze the success of eurosceptic and far-right parties in recent EU polls, prompting calls for a reduction in Brussels' power. The center-right EPP, Socialists, and ALDE Liberals maintain the largest seats in the new assembly, while anti-EU parties aim to weaken the EU from within. Voter turnout slightly increases, indicating a potential shift in EU disinterest. Financial markets respond positively to the election outcomes."
summary.5746: France's Hollande wants to change EU focus: "French President Francois Hollande pledges to push for EU reforms focusing on growth, jobs, and investment after the National Front's victory in European elections. While the elections signal a need for European governments to address public demands, the end of the EU is not imminent.
summary.5752: Jury finds cleric al-Masri guilty in terror trial: A federal jury in New York found radical Islamic cleric Abu Hamza al-Masri guilty of aiding terrorists in incidents spanning from a remote Oregon ranch to the Arabian Peninsula. Al-Masri faced 11 criminal counts, including aiding kidnappers in Yemen, sending recruits to jihadists in Afghanistan, violating U.S. sanctions against the Taliban, and attempting to establish a training camp in the U.S. He was convicted on all counts after a 12-hour deliberation. France will roll out the red carpet to British investors who will flee their country if they vote to leave the EU, as companies need Europe, Montebourg told MetroNews freesheet. Cameron's party was pushed into third place by UKIP in last week's European elections, prompting him to pledge a referendum on Britain's EU membership. summary.5758: Merkel says European parties should win voters back: Merkel says European parties should win voters back. summary.5760: Uber: The app that takes you for a ride: Uber, the global car-summoning app, connects riders to drivers through smartphone applications, expanding to over 70 cities since its 2009 founding. summary.5777: Poet Maya Angelou dies aged 86: Poet Maya Angelou dies aged 86. The Clock Runs Out on Immigration Reform: The Clock Runs Out on Immigration Reform
President Barack Obama, accompanied by Vice President Joe Biden, speaks about immigration reform, Monday, June 30, 2014. Time hasn't been on President Barack Obama's side. Once again, President Barack Obama tried to reach a deal with Republicans on one of his signature legislative priorities -- and once again, the passage of time only seemed to make a deal more unlikely. Well after virtually everyone else, President Barack Obama on Monday declared his efforts to win immigration legislation dead. As he did during his gun-control push in 2013, he tried giving Republicans time and political space to reach a deal. And like that effort, this ended with an angry president expressing his disappointment with Congress during an afternoon Rose Garden address. The longer the House waited to act after Senate passed its immigration bill, chance of a deal became less likely. On Monday, President Barack Obama said House Speaker John Boehner (R., Ohio) told him last week there would be no vote on immigration this year. "For more than a year, Republicans in the House of Representatives have refused to allow an up-or-down vote on that Senate bill or any legislation to fix our broken immigration system," President Barack Obama said. "And I held off on pressuring them for a long time to give Speaker Boehner the space he needed to get his fellow Republicans on board." This was not unlike President Barack Obama's April 2013 speech marking the background checks bill that failed to pass a Senate filibuster. President Barack Obama touched all his familiar angry and disappointed notes: The American people are with him, Republicans refuse to listen to their constituents and deep down, people who publicly oppose a broad immigration reform would rather do what he wants. "Our country and our economy would be stronger today if House Republicans had allowed a simple yes-or-no vote on this bill or, for that matter, any bill," President Barack Obama said. "They'd be following the will of the majority of the American people, who support reform. And instead they've proven again and again that they're unwilling to stand up to the tea party in order to do what's best for the country. And the worst part about it is, a bunch of them know better." Mr. Boehner, for his part, said he told President Barack Obama -- at a White House event to honor pro golfers last week -- that there can be no deal because "the American people and their elected officials don't trust him to enforce the law as written." President Barack Obama called that argument hogwash. "There are others in the Republican caucus in the House who are arguing that they can't act because they're mad at me about using my executive authority too broadly," President Barack Obama said. "This also makes no sense." There were few political recriminations for President Barack Obama after the gun-control failure, though he recently called it his biggest disappointment. But he faces enormous pressure from immigration advocates to take executive action to reduce the number of deportations. President Barack Obama hinted - again, as he did when pressure spiked in March - that he will direct subordinates to "identify additional actions my administration can take on our own," but his administration told advocates as recently as last week not to expect broad unilateral action. Pablo Alvarado, the president of the National Day Laborer Organizing Network, which has been among the loudest agitators for President Barack Obama to act without Congress, called Monday "a pivotal moment in the movement for migrant rights." "In de-linking his immigration policy from his legislative reform strategy, the president is now free to do the right thing, and he can fulfill the promise of being a transformative president," Mr. Alvarado said. "The president's enforcement-first strategy and his misguided deportation policy were premised on the possibility of legislative reform, but it is now very clear Congress itself is broken." In his remarks Monday, President Barack Obama said he expects recommendations from Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson and Attorney General Eric Holder by "the end of the summer, and I intend to adopt these recommendations without delay."

summary.6497: Here's How Tibetans Cope In High Altitudes: Tibetans have adapted to high altitudes due to a gene inherited from Denisovans, a human species that went extinct 40,000-50,000 years ago. The study, led by Rasmus Nielsen from UC Berkeley, confirms that Tibetans obtained this gene from Denisovans, demonstrating how humans evolved and adapted by acquiring genes from other species. The prevalence of this gene variant was first reported in Tibetans in 2010, based on genome sequencing. Nielsen highlights the importance of sequencing DNA from various species to uncover more genetic adaptations.

It was the second time in 13 years Argentina has been ruled in default, and served as a bad omen for the success of a marathon negotiation underway in New York with the stubborn creditors. Economy Minister Axel Kicillof was expected to emerge from the talks to give a news conference in New York after the deadline for making a $539 million payment on Argentina's restructured debt expired. Argentina had deposited the sum -- for payment to those bond holders who had accepted a write-down in deals reached in 2005 and 2010 -- in a bank account when it was due at the end of June. But a New York judge blocked the bank from forwarding the payment to the restructured creditors unless it also paid two US hedge funds the full value of their bonds, $1.3 billion, at the same time. Argentina and these funds -- NML Capital and Aurelius Capital Management -- have spent the last two days locked in talks in New York with a US court-appointed mediator to try a set a deal on payments before the expiration of a 30-day grace period. S&P's designation of "selective default" acknowledges that Argentina is current on payments to some creditors and is probably able to make some payments on the debt it has defaulted. It also said it could remove the default label once the country makes the payment on the restructured bonds. Buenos Aires has until the end of Wednesday to resolve its dispute with the so-called "holdout" hedge funds. These funds bought Argentine debt cheaply when Buenos Aires was in difficulty, and refused to accept a write-down when Latin America's third-largest economy defaulted in 2001. Kicillof is now holding last-ditch talks with the US court-appointed mediator tasked with resolving the standoff, lawyer Dan Pollack. Buenos Aires has insisted the only possible solution is for US District Judge Thomas Griesa to suspend his ruling in favor of the hedge funds. Kicillof, who flew in from Venezuela to add his weight to the negotiations, vowed after Tuesday's talks to "work at this with every bit of serious attention the issue deserves." Pollack said there had been a "frank exchange of views and concerns." Buenos Aires says paying the holdouts, which it calls "vulture funds," could expose it to claims for up to $100 billion from creditors who had previously agreed to take a 70-percent haircut. If Argentina pays the hedge funds in full, as Griesa has ruled, the 2005 and 2010 debt restructuring deals -- in which creditors accepted a 70-percent write-down -- could fall apart. The 92 percent of creditors who agreed to take a haircut could launch claims for equal treatment under what is called a Rights Upon Future Offers, or RUFO, clause. The RUFO clause expires at the end of the year, leaving Argentina scrambling to find a way to placate the holdouts until then. Markets were however hopeful for a last-minute deal. Argentine stocks closed up nearly seven percent on Wednesday. Analysts have warned a default would deepen the economic malaise gripping Argentina, exacerbating its already troubling inflation -- prices rose 15 percent in the first half of the year -- and perhaps forcing another devaluation of the peso, already devalued 20 percent in January. A default would also likely prolong Argentina's isolation from international capital markets, which it has been locked out of since halting payments on its more than $100 billion in foreign debt in 2001. That default, the largest in history at the time, plunged Argentina into an economic and social crisis that it is still battling to overcome. The global consequences of a new default would however be far smaller than in 2001, analysts say, as Argentina has since been isolated from world financial markets.

10 things to know on the Whopper - POLITICO.com: 1. The Whopper was introduced by Burger King in 1957 at the chain's first restaurant in Miami. It originally sold for 37 cents, according to The Sun-Sentinel. Today, though the price depends on the region, most Whoppers cost $3.50.

2. Burger King's co founder, Jim McLamore created the Whopper to compete with other rival restaurants who were selling larger burgers, The Washington Post reported in 2012. In his autobiography, McLamore said he chose the name because he knew it "would convey imagery of something big," the newspaper said.

3. The Whopper contains a quarter-pound patty, and according to Burger King, the restaurant serves more than 11 million customers every day. Burger King, founded in 1954, as of 2013 has 13,667 restaurants in over 95 countries. 

4. In May, Burger King told CNN Money that 5,000 locations would expand their breakfast menus to include, among other items, the Whopper.

5. As part of its 50th anniversary in Puerto Rico last year, an agency created a video promoting hands-free Whopper holders. However, debunking the video, Burger King said in a statement that the holders were not being produced or distributed by the chain, CNBC reported. 

6. How many friends is it worth losing to get a free Whopper? One promotion by Burger King in 2009 put the value at 10 Facebook friendships. Called Whopper Sacrifice, the burger chain's Facebook application gave users a coupon for a free burger if they deleted 10 Facebook friendships, according to The New York Times. However, Burger King deleted the application after Facebook requested changes; ultimately 234,000 people were de-friended.

8. Burger King opened Whopper Bar locations, an attempt to provide customers with a casual dining experience with open kitchens, The New York Times reported in 2008. However, DNAinfo reported in 2012 that the New York location -- first opened in 2010 -- had been shut down several times after failing health inspections. 

9. Burger King admitted in 2013 that some of its beef patties in the United Kingdom and Ireland contained horsemeat, The Guardian reported at the time. After testing at the production plant showed small traces of horse DNA, the company ended its contract with the plant. 

10. Burger King launched the "Proud Whopper" last month as part of San Francisco's LGBT Pride celebrations, TIME reported. When customers asked what made Proud Whoppers different, the reply from employees was "I don't know." Then the burgers were served in a Pride flag wrapper, it contained the message, "We are all the same inside."

summary.9289: ​German euroskeptics surge in two more state parliaments: German euroskeptics surge in two more state parliaments as the 'Alternative for Germany' party wins 10.1 percent in Thuringia and 11.9 percent in Brandenburg. The party now has seats in three state assemblies and is predicted to enter Germany's federal parliament after the 2017 general election. The party's message has broadened beyond opposing eurozone bailouts to include education and security. Chancellor Angela Merkel's CDU won 34.4 percent in Thuringia, but it's uncertain if they will remain in power. Europe has seen a rise in right-wing and eurosceptic parties after the EU parliamentary elections in May.

summary.9291: Celebrations for euroskeptics, coalition uncertainty for Merkel's CDU in eastern parliaments: Germany's euroskeptic Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has secured seats in three state parliaments - Thuringia, Brandenburg, and Saxony. AfD supporters celebrated election gains in Brandenburg and Thuringia, winning 12 percent and 10 percent of the vote, respectively. The party's policies include opposition to eurozone bailouts and the euro currency. In Brandenburg, the ruling Social Democrats (SPD) retained power with 32 percent of the votes. In Thuringia, the Christian Democrats won the most votes with 33.5 percent, but coalition uncertainty remains as the SPD must decide whether to align with the CDU or the Left party. Voter turnout was low in both states.

summary.9301: Anti-euro party set for gains in German state polls: Anti-euro party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), is expected to win seats in state elections in Thuringia and Brandenburg, posing a threat to Chancellor Angela Merkel's conservatives. The party, led by Bernd Lucke, narrowly missed entering the national parliament last year and won seven seats in the European Parliament. AfD's platform includes leaving the euro and emphasizing populist ideas. Analysts predict AfD will attract protest votes in the former East, where economic disparities persist. The party aims to position itself to the right of Merkel's Christian Democrats without aligning with far-right groups. The far-left Linke party is also expected to make gains in the elections.

summary.9313: Editorial: Labour's NZ Inc has little merit or substance: The Labour Party's plan to establish a $100 million-a-year sovereign wealth fund called NZ Inc to invest in "strategic" assets, including clean energy, lacks substance and merit. The fund would be funded by diverting dividends from partly privatised state-owned companies and potentially increasing oil and gas royalties. Managed by the New Zealand Super Fund board, NZ Inc would have limited autonomy in investment decisions, with politicians having some influence. However, the narrow scope and potential limitations of the fund raise concerns about its success compared to the Super Fund. Labour's proposal to increase oil and gas royalties and hold state-owned enterprise assets through "KiwiShare" may face challenges and could hinder long-term growth. The article questions the feasibility and effectiveness of NZ Inc, suggesting that private investors or the Super Fund may be better suited for such investments.
